name: Standard Image Compression Formats
text:
# Standard Image Compression Formats


## Overview
This family covers standard image [compression](#4-compression.md) codecs adapted for volumetric data, focusing on lossy block-based methods that provide hardware-accelerated random access. It sets itself apart from transform-based methods like [Wavelet and Transform-based Compression](6879-wavelet-and-transform-based-compression.md) by operating on fixed or variable spatial blocks rather than global frequency transforms, and from pure [quantization](#5935-quantization.md) methods by embedding the quantization within a standardized block format (e.g., BC7, [ASTC](#5729-astc.md)) that supports interpolation.

## Shared principles
The family shares the mechanism of dividing the data domain into discrete blocks (typically 2D or 3D) and encoding each block using a predefined format that stores endpoints (base values) and indices (weights). These formats are designed for hardware support, allowing decompression on-the-fly without storing the full decompressed volume in memory. The core mathematical operation is typically a linear interpolation between base values using stored weights.

## Subtopics

### [Variable-Block Color Compression](1878-variable-block-color-compression.md)
[Variable-Block Color Compression](#1878-variable-block-color-compression.md) is a lossy compression method for sparse 3D color data that groups voxels into variable-length blocks to optimize the compression ratio. It sets itself apart from fixed-size block methods by allowing block boundaries to adapt to local color similarity, thereby reducing the number of headers required for large homogeneous regions while maintaining a strict error threshold. See [Variable-Block Color Compression](1878-variable-block-color-compression.md).

### [ASTC](5729-astc.md)
ASTC is a flexible, hardware-supported fixed-rate lossy compression method that uses various block-size configurations to cover a wide range of bit rates. It solves the problem of limited bandwidth in real-time rendering by allowing on-the-fly decompression of volumetric data directly from compressed coordinates without storing the entire decompressed volume in memory. Unlike its sibling [Variable-Block Color Compression](1878-variable-block-color-compression.md), which handles segmented datasets with splitting planes, ASTC is an adaptation of Block Truncated Coding (BTC) that shares similarities with [S3TC](#5727-fixed-rate-block-coding-vtc-s3tc.md) and supports hardware-accelerated random access. See [ASTC](5729-astc.md).

### Block-Dictionary Compression
- **Definition**: Optional compression for distribution where the BC7 stream is compressed with a block dictionary [S1, unofficial].
- **Steps**: Cut atlas into 4 × 4 texel blocks. K-means clustering builds a codebook of K = 65,536 block centroids. Each centroid is encoded as one 16-byte BC7 block. Every atlas block stores a 16-bit codebook index. Load time: Indices are gathered back into a dense BC7 stream, so the renderer is unchanged and keeps a single hardware bilinear fetch per fragment [S1, unofficial].
- **Numbers**: Codebook size: 1 MB. Index size: 2 bytes per block. Reduction: 7.0× of the atlas payload (173 MB to 24.7 MB on average for [Mip-NeRF 360](#3306-mip-nerf-360.md)). Complete web bundle size: 38.4 MB (dictionary atlas with 8-bit surfels (FP16 positions) and cameras) [S1, unofficial].
- **Comparison**: The dictionary reduces download size, while GPU memory and frame time are those of the raw BC7 atlas [S1, unofficial].

### BC7 Quantization with Empirical Range
- **Definition**: Compression of the baked atlas using BC7 [block compression](#2453-block-compression.md). The residual range is estimated empirically to avoid [clipping](#1444-clipping.md) heavy tails, and the scale is snapped to align zero residual with an integer quantization level [S1, unofficial].
- **Steps**: 1. Estimate residual range as empirical [min, max] with a 2% margin over ~1.3 million samples (64 random UV positions on 20,000 surfels). 2. Quantize uniformly with a single global (offset, scale) pair. 3. Snap scale so residual zero coincides with an integer quantization level. 4. Pad data to RGBA to match BC7 4x4 block layout (16 bytes per block, 1 byte per texel) [S1, unofficial].
- **Pitfalls**: Using range estimates of the form $\mu \pm k\sigma$ clips heavy tails, dimming bright peaks uniformly. Using the full empirical range avoids this. If the scale is not snapped to align zero residual with an integer level, halfstep rounding bias propagates through the outer ReLU of Eq. 2, systematically dimming pixels near the activation threshold [S1, unofficial].
- **Numbers**: BC7 RGBA storage uses 1 byte/texel (~173 MB mean atlas size) with ±0.01 dB PSNR change compared to neural FP16 RGB (6 bytes/texel, ~1039 MB) [S1, unofficial].

## Background
Standard image compression formats like BC7 and ASTC originated in the graphics hardware industry to compress texture data for efficient GPU access. BC7 was introduced by S3 Texture Compression (S3TC) and later standardized in OpenGL and DirectX. ASTC (Adaptive Scalable Texture Compression) was developed by ARM to provide flexible block sizes. Their application to volume rendering and [splatting](#23-splatting.md) (e.g., in Mip-NeRF 360 contexts) is a recent adaptation, leveraging their hardware support for random access decompression to handle large spatial atlases [S1, S2].
